📖 Networking Basics for Year 9

Click a concept to explore it.

Australia's NBN (National Broadband Network)

The NBN is Australia's national wholesale broadband infrastructure, designed to provide high-speed internet access to all Australians.

NBN Technologies:
  • Fibre to the Premises (FTTP)
  • Fibre to the Node (FTTN)
  • Fixed Wireless
  • Satellite (Sky Muster, for remote areas)
Impact on Routing:
  • Faster domestic connections
  • Better quality for streaming
  • Reduced latency within Australia
  • More reliable internet access

🔍 How does tracert actually work?

The Route Tracer tab visualises what the real tracert (Windows) / traceroute (Mac & Linux) command does. Here's the clever trick behind it:

1. Time To Live (TTL)

Every packet carries a TTL counter. Each router that forwards the packet subtracts 1. When TTL hits 0, the router throws the packet away — this stops lost packets circling the internet forever.

2. Deliberate expiry

Traceroute sends a packet with TTL=1 (dies at the first router), then TTL=2 (dies at the second), then TTL=3… Each router that kills a packet sends back an ICMP "Time Exceeded" message — revealing its IP address!

3. Map the path

Collecting those replies, hop by hop, reveals every router between you and the destination — plus how long each round trip took. Try it yourself: open a terminal and type tracert google.com
Why can't a web page run a real traceroute? Browsers aren't allowed to craft raw packets with custom TTL values — that would be a security risk. So the Route Tracer tab does the next best thing: it performs real DNS and location lookups, then simulates the in-between hops using the real geography of submarine cables and internet exchanges.

🔢 More about IP Addresses — Year 9 Guide

What is an IP Address?

An IP (Internet Protocol) address is like a postal address for devices on the internet. Just like your home has a unique address so mail can find you, every device connected to the internet has a unique IP address so data can find it.

Think of it this way: if the internet is a massive city, IP addresses are the street addresses that help data packets find their way to the right "house" (device).

IPv4 Address Structure

The Dotted Decimal Format

192.168.1.1
  • Four numbers separated by dots
  • Each number is called an "octet"
  • Each octet ranges from 0 to 255
  • Total of 32 bits (8 bits per octet)

Why 0–255?

Each octet is 8 bits, and with 8 bits you can represent:

2⁸ = 256 different values
(0, 1, 2, 3, … 254, 255)

🤔 Why Do We Need Different IP Address Formats?

  • Browser compatibility: some browsers and systems understand IPs in different formats — you can type "2130706433" instead of "127.0.0.1"!
  • Computer processing: computers actually work in binary (1s and 0s), so binary shows how computers "think" about IP addresses.
  • Network troubleshooting: network engineers sometimes use hexadecimal or octal for easier calculation and debugging.
  • Understanding technology: learning these conversions helps you understand how digital systems work at a fundamental level.

🎯 Practice Exercises

Convert each decimal number to the requested number system. Use the calculator above to help with divisions and remainders!

💡 Exercise Tips

  • Binary: repeated division by 2, write remainders from bottom to top
  • Octal: repeated division by 8, write remainders from bottom to top
  • Hexadecimal: repeated division by 16 — remember A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15
  • Padding: binary should be 8 digits, octal 3 digits, hexadecimal 2 digits

🚀 Try This at Home!

Browser experiment: try typing these in your browser's address bar:

  • 127.0.0.1  (dotted decimal)
  • 2130706433  (decimal as a single number)
  • 0x7f000001  (hexadecimal)
  • 017700000001  (octal)

They all point to the same place — your own computer!

Number System Quick Reference

Binary (Base 2):0, 1
Octal (Base 8):0–7
Decimal (Base 10):0–9
Hexadecimal (Base 16):0–9, A–F

Powers of 2 (for Binary)

2⁰ = 1
2¹ = 2
2² = 4
2³ = 8
2⁴ = 16
2⁵ = 32
2⁶ = 64
2⁷ = 128

🎯 Key Takeaways

  • IP addresses are unique identifiers for devices on the internet
  • The same IP address can be written in different number systems
  • Computers work with binary, but humans prefer decimal
  • Understanding these conversions helps you understand how computers work
